title: Mining the microbial dark matter: how we find dehalogenases
author: MGB Lab
description: More than 99% of microbial species have never been grown in a laboratory. This post describes how metagenomic sequencing lets us access their genetic repertoire — and why this matters for PFAS biodegradation research.
body:
Most of the microbial world has never been seen in a Petri dish. The techniques that built classical microbiology — isolation, culture, growth — fundamentally miss the vast majority of environmental microbes, sometimes called the *microbial dark matter*.

## The cultivation bottleneck

Fewer than 1% of environmental microorganisms can be cultured under standard laboratory conditions. This means that for every enzyme we know about from cultured organisms, there are potentially hundreds of functional equivalents hiding in uncultivated lineages.

For PFAS biodegradation research, this bottleneck is critical. The enzymes most capable of breaking C–F bonds may belong to organisms we have never grown.

## How metagenomics bypasses the bottleneck

Metagenomics bypasses this bottleneck entirely. Instead of culturing organisms, we extract DNA directly from environmental samples — soil cores, river sediments, contaminated groundwater — and sequence everything present. A single sample can yield hundreds of millions of reads representing thousands of species.

## Our computational pipeline

The computational challenge is then enormous: from this raw sequence data, we must identify open reading frames, predict protein function, and rank candidates by their likelihood of catalysing C–F bond cleavage.

Our custom pipelines combine:

- **Hidden Markov Model (HMM) searches** against curated dehalogenase families
- **Structural homology** using AlphaFold-predicted models
- **Machine learning classifiers** trained on known dehalogenase families

## Results

The result is a ranked list of enzyme candidates — many from organisms that have never been cultured — ready for structural modelling and experimental validation.

In our most recent dataset of 3.2 million environmental protein sequences, we identified over 400 high-confidence dehalogenase candidates, of which roughly 60% came from completely uncultivated lineages.
